replacements.before:
Recent coding agents have made tool-using, stateful execution prominent.
The same execution style is increasingly used for knowledge work that ends in long-form documents.
Yet long-form writing systems usually advance an outline, task graph, or fixed stage sequence rather than deciding which writing process is needed next.
Drawing on cognitive process theory, we propose \condAgenticCogWriter, which maintains a shared draft, goals, and process history while a Monitor agent chooses and delegates planning, drafting, or reviewing.
We evaluate our system across three long-form writing benchmarks using pointwise rubric scoring and pairwise same-prompt preference judgments.
Pre-specified per-benchmark pairwise tests separate our system from one-shot generation in most cases but from a fixed planning--drafting--revision workflow and adaptive task planning in fewer than half, and a post-hoc prompt-level summary across benchmarks favors it over all three.
Its paired pointwise differences favor it over all three alternatives on WritingBench and on HelloBench's native rubric, and ablations that drop explicit goals or fix the process order keep most of this advantage.
In process traces, \AfourCycleCompliantRate\ of complete paths conform to the planning--drafting--reviewing cycle structure, and \AfourReviewingToTranslatingRate\ and \AfourReviewingToPlanningRate\ of runs return from reviewing to drafting and to planning, respectively.
replacements.after:
Recent coding agents have made tool-using, stateful execution prominent, and the same style increasingly serves knowledge work ending in long-form documents.
Yet long-form writing systems usually advance an outline, task graph, or fixed stage sequence rather than deciding which writing process is needed next.
Drawing on cognitive process theory, we propose \condAgenticCogWriter, which maintains a shared draft, goals, and process history while a Monitor agent chooses and delegates planning, drafting, or reviewing.
We evaluate our system across three long-form writing benchmarks using pointwise rubric scores and pairwise same-prompt preference judgments.
Pre-specified per-benchmark pairwise tests separate our system from one-shot generation in most cases but from a fixed planning--drafting--revision workflow and adaptive task planning in fewer than half, and a post-hoc prompt-level summary favors it over all three.
Its paired pointwise differences favor it over all three alternatives on WritingBench and HelloBench's native rubric, and ablations dropping explicit goals or fixing the process order keep most of this advantage.
A post-hoc fixed workflow with our role instructions does not reproduce the preference.
In process traces, \AfourCycleCompliantRate\ of complete paths conform to the planning--drafting--reviewing cycle structure, and only \AfourReviewingToPlanningRate\ of runs return from reviewing to planning, while \AfourReviewingToTranslatingRate\ return to drafting.

Pointwise rubric scoring and pairwise same-prompt preference evaluation assess document quality from complementary perspectives.
In pre-specified per-benchmark pairwise tests, our system is preferred to one-shot generation in \PooledFourOneHolmCellsTotal\ of nine tests and to a fixed writing pipeline and adaptive task planning in \PooledFourTwoHolmCellsTotal\ and \PooledFourThreeHolmCellsTotal, while a post-hoc prompt-level summary across benchmarks favors it over all three.
The component analyses support a system-level interpretation: ablations that drop explicit goals or fix the process order keep most of this advantage over the alternatives.
Process traces show that \AfourCycleCompliantRate\ of complete paths conform to the planning--drafting--reviewing cycle structure and that \AfourReviewingToPlanningRate\ of runs return from reviewing to planning, so adaptive ordering is seldom used.
replacements.after:

The component analyses support a system-level interpretation: ablations that drop explicit goals or fix the process order keep most of this advantage over the alternatives, and adding our role instructions to the fixed pipeline post hoc does not reproduce it.

Because each decision is made from the updated state, the process order is not fixed: drafting can expose a structural problem that sends control back to planning, and reviewing can trigger another drafting or planning pass.
For example, if \texttt{Reviewing} finds that the draft omits a section the task requires, the \texttt{Monitor} can select \texttt{Planning} to add a goal for that section before further \texttt{Translating}.
The \texttt{Monitor} may stop after any process and return the current draft as the final document $D_{\mathrm{final}}$; the runner's output-token budget or per-command timeout can also end a run before a \texttt{Reviewing} pass.

The primary evaluator belongs to the same model family as the generator, and related generator--judge models can exhibit preference leakage or self-preference~\citep{li2026preference,panickssery2024selfpreference}.
The cross-family judge rescored one generation run for the contrasts with \condSinglePass, \condTaskPlanning, and \condNoGoals; summing W/L/T counts over the three benchmarks leaves all three favoring our system, but the judge produces many ties and reverses 3 of 9 benchmark-level comparisons, and its agreement with the primary judge is $\kappa=\JudgeAgreementKappa$ over all \JudgeAgreementPairs\ prompt-level outcomes and $\kappa=\JudgeAgreementDecidedKappa$ over the \JudgeAgreementDecidedPairs\ pairs both judges decide.
Extending the check to \condStaged\ and \condFixedOrder\ and to all three generation runs would cover every contrast between our system and an alternative or ablation.
Model-judge preference is not human preference; a blinded human comparison of same-prompt outputs, stratified by benchmark, contrast, and prompt length, would measure judge agreement with human readers.
replacements.after:
The primary evaluator belongs to the same model family as the generator, and related generator--judge models can exhibit preference leakage or self-preference~\citep{li2026preference,panickssery2024selfpreference}.
The cross-family judge rescored one generation run for every contrast between our system and an alternative or ablation; summing W/L/T counts over the three benchmarks favors our system over \condStaged\ (\CrossFamilyFullStagedWinRate, $p=\CrossFamilyFullStagedP$) and leaves \condFixedOrder\ near parity (\CrossFamilyFullFixedOrderWinRate, $p=\CrossFamilyFullFixedOrderP$), as under the primary judge.
The judge produces many ties and reverses 5 of 15 benchmark-level comparisons, and its agreement with the primary judge is $\kappa=\JudgeAgreementKappa$ over all \JudgeAgreementPairs\ prompt-level outcomes and $\kappa=\JudgeAgreementDecidedKappa$ over the \JudgeAgreementDecidedPairs\ pairs both judges decide; extending it to all three generation runs is the next step.
Model-judge preference is not human preference; a blinded human comparison of same-prompt outputs, stratified by benchmark, contrast, and prompt length, would measure judge agreement with human readers.

\subsection{Cross-Family Judge Robustness}
\label{app:cross-family}
Table~\ref{tab:appendix-cross-family} reports benchmark-level results for three cross-family robustness contrasts involving our system.
Within each contrast, summing W/L/T counts over the three benchmarks gives \CrossFamilyFullSinglePassWLT\ versus \condSinglePass, \CrossFamilyFullTaskPlanningWLT\ versus \condTaskPlanning, and \CrossFamilyFullNoGoalsWLT\ versus \condNoGoals.
The corresponding Wilson intervals are \CrossFamilyFullSinglePassInterval, \CrossFamilyFullTaskPlanningInterval, and \CrossFamilyFullNoGoalsInterval.
Across all three selected contrasts and benchmarks, the judge yields a non-tied order-consistent outcome on \CrossFamilyPooledCommitRate\ of \CrossFamilyPooledN\ eligible pairs, with \CrossFamilyPooledWLT\ W/L/T; \CrossFamilyPooledAgreement\ prompt-level outcomes agree with the same-family judge.
Cohen's kappa between the two judges is \JudgeAgreementKappa\ over these outcomes, most of which are cross-family ties, and \JudgeAgreementDecidedKappa\ over the \JudgeAgreementDecidedPairs\ pairs both judges decide, of which \JudgeAgreementDecidedAgreeing\ agree.
